steps.title: What is DigiD?
steps.body: DigiD is your personal digital identity for the Dutch government. It proves who you are online, for example with the Tax Office, your municipality, or your health insurer.

steps.title: Logging in with the DigiD app
steps.body:
1. Install the free DigiD app on your phone (one time, ideally with help from family)
  2. On the computer, go to the website where you want to log in and choose 'Log in with DigiD'
  3. Open the DigiD app on your phone and scan the code, or follow the instructions in the app
  4. Confirm with your face, fingerprint, or PIN

steps.title: What is DigiD used for?
steps.body: For example: filing a tax return, making an appointment with your municipality, arranging your health insurance, or logging in to MijnOverheid.

steps.title: Staying safe with DigiD
steps.body:
Important: DigiD is just as personal as your bank card.

  • Never share your DigiD login details or code with anyone, not even family
  • The government will never call you asking for your DigiD code — that is always a scam
  • Not sure about a message or call? Don't respond, hang up, and check with family

steps.title: Explore
steps.body: Browse the official DigiD information page below. Don't log in with your own DigiD during class — practice that at home with family instead.

steps.title: What is MijnOverheid?
steps.body: MijnOverheid is your personal mailbox for the government. Here you'll find official letters, your personal details, and ongoing matters, such as an application with your municipality.

steps.title: Logging in and the message box
steps.body:
1. Go to mijnoverheid.nl and click 'Log in'
  2. Log in with DigiD
  3. Click 'Messages' to read your digital mail, for example from the Tax Office

steps.title: What else can you find there?
steps.body: Under 'Personal details' you can see what the government knows about you (address, family situation). Under 'Ongoing matters' you can see the status of applications you've submitted.

steps.title: Exercise
steps.body: Browse the MijnOverheid website below. Only log in at home, together with family, if you have your own DigiD.

steps.title: What is online banking?
steps.body: Online banking lets you manage your bank affairs through your bank's website or app: checking your balance, transferring money, viewing statements. This is usually done through your bank's app on your phone.

steps.title: Logging in to your bank
steps.body: Most banks use their app together with a PIN, face recognition, or fingerprint. Some banks still use a separate 'scanner' device that reads a code from your bank card.

steps.title: Checking a payment
steps.body:
Always check carefully before confirming a payment:

  • Is the account number or recipient's name correct?
  • Is the amount correct?

Once confirmed, a payment usually cannot be reversed.

steps.title: Recognizing bank helpdesk fraud
steps.body: Your bank will never call you asking for your PIN, DigiD code, or to transfer money 'for your own safety'. Get such a call? Hang up and call your bank yourself using the official number from their website or your bank card.

steps.title: What is phishing?
steps.body: Phishing is a fake email, text message, or chat that looks real (for example from your bank, a delivery company, or the tax office), but is meant to steal your password, PIN, or money.

steps.title: Warning signs
steps.body:
• The sender's address isn't quite right (for example tax-office-nl.com instead of the real domain)
  • Spelling and grammar mistakes
  • You're pressured to act fast ('within 24 hours, or else...')
  • A link that doesn't seem to go to the real website

steps.title: What to do with a suspicious message
steps.body:
1. Don't click the link and don't open the attachment
  2. Go to the official website yourself by typing the address, instead of clicking the link
  3. Not sure? Check with family, or call the organization yourself using a number you looked up yourself
  4. Delete the suspicious message

steps.title: Exercise: an inbox full of fake emails
steps.body:
Below is an inbox with six recreated example emails — some are phishing, some are simply safe. Open each one, read it carefully, and choose at the bottom whether you think it’s safe or suspicious.

From: PostNL <delivery@postnl-track-parcel.info>
To: you@example.com
Subject: Delivery failed: reschedule within 24 hours

Dear customer,

Unfortunately we were unable to deliver your parcel. There is an outstanding amount of €0.49 in shipping costs. Pay this within 24 hours or your parcel will be returned to the sender.

(example — in real life this would link to a fake site; never actually click a button like this)

✅ Correct!

Correctly flagged as phishing. The signs you spotted:

  • The full email address isn’t PostNL’s: postnl-track-parcel.info
  • A tiny amount, designed to lower your guard
  • Time pressure (“within 24 hours”)
  • Delivery services never ask you to pay extra online via a link in an email

⚠️ That was wrong

This is a classic parcel-delivery scam. The signs you missed:

  • The full email address isn’t PostNL’s: postnl-track-parcel.info
  • A tiny amount, designed to lower your guard
  • Time pressure (“within 24 hours”)
  • Delivery services never ask you to pay extra online via a link in an email
From: ING Bank <security@ing-verify-online.com>
To: you@example.com
Subject: Important: your account will be blocked within 24 hours

Dear customer,

We have detected unusual activity on your account. To protect it, please re-verify your details within 24 hours. Failing to do so will result in your account being automatically blocked.

(example — in real life this would link to a fake site; never actually click a button like this)

✅ Correct!

Correctly flagged as phishing. The signs you spotted:

  • A bank always uses your real name, never “Dear customer”
  • The domain isn’t your bank’s real one, but ing-verify-online.com
  • Threatening a block within 24 hours creates pressure
  • Your bank never asks you to “verify” via a link in an email — always log in yourself via the app or a site you type in yourself

⚠️ That was wrong

This is a classic bank phishing email. The signs you missed:

  • A bank always uses your real name, never “Dear customer”
  • The domain isn’t your bank’s real one, but ing-verify-online.com
  • Threatening a block within 24 hours creates pressure
  • Your bank never asks you to “verify” via a link in an email — always log in yourself via the app or a site you type in yourself
From: Microsoft Account Team <account-security@microsoft-support-verify.net>
To: you@example.com
Subject: Unusual sign-in detected — action required

Hello,

We noticed a sign-in to your account from a new device. If this wasn’t you, secure your account within 1 hour, or access to your account will be revoked.

(example — in real life this would link to a fake site; never actually click a button like this)

✅ Correct!

Correctly flagged as phishing. The signs you spotted:

  • The domain isn’t microsoft.com but microsoft-support-verify.net
  • Extreme time pressure (“within 1 hour”) is a classic trick
  • A generic greeting (“Hello”) instead of your real name
  • Not sure? Log in yourself at account.microsoft.com (typed in yourself) to check your security — never via a link in an email

⚠️ That was wrong

This is a fake security alert. The signs you missed:

  • The domain isn’t microsoft.com but microsoft-support-verify.net
  • Extreme time pressure (“within 1 hour”) is a classic trick
  • A generic greeting (“Hello”) instead of your real name
  • Not sure? Log in yourself at account.microsoft.com (typed in yourself) to check your security — never via a link in an email
From: National Gift Promotion <winners@prize-payout-claim.com>
To: you@example.com
Subject: 🎉 Congratulations! You’ve won an iPhone 17 Pro

Congratulations!

You have been randomly selected as the winner of a free iPhone 17 Pro in our anniversary giveaway. To claim your prize, simply pay the shipping fee (€4.95) and enter your bank details for verification.

(example — in real life this would link to a fake site; never actually click a button like this)

✅ Correct!

Correctly flagged as phishing. The signs you spotted:

  • You never entered this “giveaway” — you can’t win something you never applied for
  • A genuine prize never asks you to pay first or enter your bank details
  • The domain prize-payout-claim.com sounds official but doesn’t really exist
  • “Too good to be true” usually is

⚠️ That was wrong

This is a classic prize scam. The signs you missed:

  • You never entered this “giveaway” — you can’t win something you never applied for
  • A genuine prize never asks you to pay first or enter your bank details
  • The domain prize-payout-claim.com sounds official but doesn’t really exist
  • “Too good to be true” usually is
From: Marieke de Vries <marieke.devries@companyname-inc.net>
To: you@example.com
Subject: Need something quick — just between us

Hi,

I’m in a meeting and can’t call. Could you quickly buy 4 gift cards of €50 for a client? Send me the codes as soon as you have them, I’ll pay you back once I can do my banking again. Keep this between us for now, I’ll explain later.

✅ Correct!

Correctly flagged as phishing. The signs you spotted:

  • Urgency + secrecy (“don’t mention this”, “keep this between us”) is a classic manipulation trick
  • An unusual request: buy gift cards and send the codes
  • “Can’t call” prevents you from double-checking
  • A colleague’s or manager’s real email almost never matches companyname-inc.net — always verify through another channel (phone, in person) before doing anything

⚠️ That was wrong

This is “CEO fraud”: someone impersonating a colleague or manager. The signs you missed:

  • Urgency + secrecy (“don’t mention this”, “keep this between us”) is a classic manipulation trick
  • An unusual request: buy gift cards and send the codes
  • “Can’t call” prevents you from double-checking
  • A colleague’s or manager’s real email almost never matches companyname-inc.net — always verify through another channel (phone, in person) before doing anything
From: Amazon <orders@amazon.com>
To: you@example.com
Subject: Your order #12345678 has shipped

Dear customer,

Good news: your order has shipped and is on its way. You can track its status via ‘Your Orders’ on amazon.com or in the Amazon app. Thanks for your order!

✅ Correct!

You correctly chose ‘safe’. The signs that confirm it:

  • The domain is genuinely correct: amazon.com
  • No urgency, no threats, no request to pay or enter details
  • Makes sense if you recently ordered something from Amazon
  • Still not sure? Log in to amazon.com separately (typed in yourself) to check your order, instead of clicking a link in the email

⚠️ That was wrong

You chose ‘safe’, but this was actually phishing. This email is actually genuinely safe — being cautious is fine, but this wasn’t phishing. The signs that it checks out:

  • The domain is genuinely correct: amazon.com
  • No urgency, no threats, no request to pay or enter details
  • Makes sense if you recently ordered something from Amazon
  • Still not sure? Log in to amazon.com separately (typed in yourself) to check your order, instead of clicking a link in the email

lessons.title: Check whether your data has already been leaked

steps.title: Why check this?
steps.body:
Large companies sometimes get hacked, exposing lists of email addresses (and sometimes passwords) — often without you noticing as a customer. That data can then be traded among criminals.

There are free, trustworthy websites where you can check whether your email address appears in one of these leaked lists.

steps.title: Checking Have I Been Pwned
steps.body:
Have I Been Pwned (haveibeenpwned.com) is a globally known, trustworthy service — built by an independent security expert and the standard for this kind of check for many years.

  1. Go to the website
  2. Type your email address in the search box
  3. Click 'pwned?'

You'll immediately see whether, and in which known data breaches, your email address has been found. Nothing about you is stored to identify you further.

steps.title: Check Je Hack from the Dutch police (optional)
steps.body: The Dutch police offer a similar, official check called Check Je Hack. This is entirely optional — you don't need to do both, but it doesn't hurt to double-check with another official source.

steps.title: Note: only use the real website
steps.body: Always type the address yourself in your browser, or use the buttons above. Did you end up on a 'check if you've been hacked' website via a link in an email or chat message? Be extra suspicious — that could itself be a phishing attempt.

steps.title: Your email address was found — now what?
steps.body:
Is your email address in one of these lists? Then there's a higher chance you'll receive phishing and scam messages by email, text, or WhatsApp — criminals know your address is 'active'.

  • Be extra alert to unexpected messages, especially ones creating urgency
  • Use a new, strong password for the leaked account (see the next steps)
  • Turn on two-factor authentication (2FA) wherever possible
  • Never reuse the same password in multiple places

Nothing found? Good — but stay alert regardless, since new leaks can always happen.

steps.title: Why a strong password?
steps.body: A weak password (like welcome123 or your date of birth) is easy for criminals to guess. A strong, unique password for each website protects your accounts.

steps.title: How to create a strong password
steps.body:
• At least 12 characters long
  • A mix of uppercase, lowercase, numbers, and symbols
  • No names, birth dates, or easily guessed words
  • A different password for every website or app

Tip: a string of 4 random words (for example Bicycle7Rain!Tree) is long, strong, and easy to remember.

steps.title: What is two-factor authentication (2FA)?
steps.body: With 2FA, you need a second confirmation besides your password to log in, for example a code sent to your phone. This means someone with just your password still can't log in.

steps.title: Setting up 2FA
steps.body: Most services (Google, Facebook, your bank) offer this under Settings > Security > Two-factor authentication. Follow the on-screen steps to link your phone number or an app.
